messages.body_plain:
Update: with off-list help from Dan and Thomas Riecke, I think I got this worked out. It works about as well as the bootstrapping approach now. Hopefully reproducible example attached (you may need to get the MigConnectivity package from the devpsi2 branch on GitHub to get some parts to work).

On Wednesday, December 29, 2021 at 1:17:06 PM UTC-5 falaf...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Dan,
>
> Thank you for the suggestion! Apologies for the lack of clarity - dest was put in that version as a latent state to link together psi and probT. Your suggestion is good where we know the target population of individual animals (e.g., telemetry data), but with the genetics data we have at best a table of probabilities, with a row for each animal, and each row summing to 1. Often one of those probabilities is quite high, but I want to incorporate the underlying uncertainty.
>
> Jeff
>
> On Wednesday, December 29, 2021 at 12:39:12 PM UTC-5 gib...@vt.edu wrote:
> > Hey Jeff,
> >
> > What about something like this? Where 'genetics' is a frequency matrix that represents the number of samples associated with each non-breeding location from each breeding area with nProbT now representing the total number of samples from a specific breeding area. It wasn't clear if 'dest' was actually data or a latent state, but if it's data (i.e., observations of marked birds from a specific breeding area on a specific non-breeding area), this approach would allow both sources of data (genetics and observations) to jointly estimate the same parameter (psi).
> >
> > for(k in 1: npop ){
> >   genetics[k,1:ndest) ~ dmulti(psi[k,1:ndest, nProbT[k])
> >
> > }
> >   dest[i] ~ dcat(psi[assO[i], 1:ndest])
> >
> > # priors
> > for(j in 1:npop){
> >   for(k in 1:ndest){
> >      m0[j, k] ~ dgamma(1, 1)
> >      psi[j, k] <- m0[j, k] / sum(m0[j, 1:ndest])
> >   } #k
> > }#j
> >
> > I've done something similar with just observations of birds (no genetic data) and it seemed to work well enough. So, I'd be surprised if this wouldn't work in the absence of a major discrepancy between the two data types.
> >
> > -Dan
> >
> > On Wed, Dec 29, 2021 at 8:19 AM falaf...@gmail.com <falaf...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > I'm trying to estimate population-level transition probabilities for migratory animals (an aspect of migratory connectivity) from a variety of data sources. I've got several data sources implemented using a bootstrapping approach (see https://github.com/SMBC-NZP/MigConnectivity), and I'm working now on Bayesian implementations. One of the simplest data types has got me stymied, for some reason. That data type is individual-level probabilities of connecting to each of the target populations (e.g., probabilities of breeding population assignment from nonbreeding genetic samples, where one is trying to estimate nonbreeding to breeding population-level transition probabilities). It seems like it should be easy - the data (probT) and parameter to be estimated (psi) are essentially the same thing, transition probabilities to target populations that sum to 1, either by individual or by origin population. But so far everything I've tried either doesn't work at all or gives very biased estimates with simulated data. This is the closest version I'm come up with so far (JAGS code):
> > > model{
> > > # likelihood
> > > for(i in 1:nProbT){
> > >   probT[i, 1:ndest] ~ ddirich(alpha[i, 1:ndest])
> > >   dest[i] ~ dcat(psi[assO[i], 1:ndest])
> > >   for (k in 1:ndest){
> > >     alpha[i, k] <- alphaPrior[i, k] + (dest[i]==k)
> > >   }#k
> > > }#i
> > >
> > > # priors
> > > for(j in 1:npop){
> > >   for(k in 1:ndest){
> > >     m0[j, k] ~ dgamma(1, 1)
> > >     psi[j, k] <- m0[j, k] / sum(m0[j, 1:ndest])
> > >   } #k
> > > }#j
> > > }
> > >
> > > where nProbT is the number of samples, ndest is the number of target populations, assO is the known origin population for each sampled animal, alphaPrior is all ones (what number I use doesn't seem to matter, unless I use all zeros, in which case I get an error), and npop is the number of origin populations. As I said, this produces very biased psi estimates (much more than the bootstrapping approach with the same data). The direction of this bias is towards making all the psis identical.
> > >
> > > Can someone suggest a better approach?
> > >
> > > Thank you very much,

messages.subject: Announcement: community occupancy models with camtrapR
messages.subject_clean: Announcement: community occupancy models with camtrapR
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
the R package camtrapR can now create community occupancy models automatically with a new function called "communityModel". It:
automatically writes model code for community occupancy models in JAGS or Nimble
sets inits and selects parameters to monitor
allows fixed and random effects
bundles all relevant input data into a convenient object (for which several methods exist)
calculates various derived quantities (e.g. residuals, Bayesian p-values, species richness)
allows for optional data augmentation (fully open community or known maximum species richness)
In addition there are methods for:
fitting models,
plotting model estimates,
plotting marginal effects,
creating predictions of occupancy probabilities and species richness (including spatial predictions)
The function is intended to be general and not restricted to camera trapping data.

It is included in the the GitHub version of camtrapR which can be installed via:
install_github("jniedballa/camtrapR", build_vignettes = TRUE)

See vignette 5 in the package for more details and examples: (based on data simulated with the AHMbook package)
vignette("camtrapr5", package = "camtrapR")

The function code is here:
https://github.com/jniedballa/camtrapR/blob/master/R/communityModel.R

Please feel free to reach out if you should have any questions. It is a first release, so things may change a little in the future. Also, there are still some limitations which will be addressed in the future, e.g. allowing customizable priors.

Best regards,

Jürgen

messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I'm building an integrated population model with monthly time steps, and I'm uncertain how to specify that productivity and survival both contribute to a population total.

For example, the juvenile population size for a lot of the breeding season is made up of new-born juveniles and those that have survived from the previous month.
So,  Nj[t] = f * Nad[t-1]  +  sj * Nj[t-1].

Normally I'd use a Poisson distribution for the productivity bit and a Binomial for the survival, so I'm wondering if the below is valid?
jpois ~ dpois(f * Nad[t-1])
jbin ~ dbin(sj, Nj[t-1])
Nj[t] <- jpois + jbin
Or if this would end up introducing issues/hidden parameters that aren't useful. If so would a Poisson distribution combining the two process be better, as in:
Nj[t] ~ dpois(f * Nad[t-1]  +  sj * Nj[t-1])

Any thoughts would be greatly appreciated!

Thank you,
Ellie Scopes

messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody,

I am trying to save time by running an occupancy dynamic community model with data in vectorial form, following page 311 (Chpt 5.4) of AHM2.

With data in a four-dimensional array, my BUGS language observation model would include the command:

 y[i,j,t,k] ~ dbern(z[i,t,k] * pg[i,j,t,k])

Of course this does not work with vectorialized data, because after vectorialization the object 'y' has only two dimensions, with 5 columns that contain numeric information on detection/non-detecion, site, survey, year, and species.

The question is how to direct jags to the correct element of the first column?

If the BUGS language had something like a 'which' command (as R does), I would use something like:

y[which(y[,2]==i & y[,3]==j & y[,4]==t & y[,5]==k),1] ~ dbern(z[i,t,k] * pg[i,j,t,k])

But this did not work, of course.

Does anyone have a solution for this? Thanks for the attention!

Gonçalo

Hi Goncalo -

I haven't looked at that section of the AHM2 code, but I think this might work:

For simplicity, I'd separate the various columns of y
ylong = y[,1]
site = y[,2]
survey = y[,3]
year = y[,4]
species = y[,5]

Then you can loop through the elements of ylong (in order) and use the site, survey, year, and species columns as indices to point to the proper element in z or pg that's associated with a particular detection/nondetection observation like:

for(s in 1:length(ylong)) {
ylong[s]  ~ dbern(z[site[s],year[s],species[s]] * pg[site[s],survey[s],year[s],species[s]])
}

You may need to fuss with the site, survey, survey, and year columns to make sure that they can be used as indices and point to the correct element of z and pg, but hopefully this general approach might address your question?

Best,
erin

Dear Goncalo, Erin,

that's great about this list: less than 60 mins you can already get an answer. I think Erin says it right, but I also wanted to point out an example of a model for long-form data in Chapter 4 of the AHM2, for a single-season dynocc model (page 269). The main relevant parts go like this, below. So: no change in the state model: you can define the latent variables in there in their usual arrayed format, which is convenient. Only change really in the observation model.

Best regards  -- Marc

# Ecological submodel: Define state conditional on parameters
for (i in 1:nsites){
  z[i,1] ~ dbern(psi1)
  for (t in 2:nyears){
    z[i,t] ~ dbern(z[i,t-1]*phi[t-1] + (1-z[i,t-1])*gamma[t-1])
  }
}
# Observation model
for (i in 1:nobs){
  logit(p[i]) <- alpha.lp[year[i]] + beta.lp.1[year[i]] * date[i] +
    beta.lp.2[year[i]] * pow(date[i],2) + eps.site[site[i], year[i]]
  y[i] ~ dbin(z[site[i],year[i]]*p[i], nsurveys[i])
}

messages.subject: what if we use latent covariates for detectability?
messages.subject_clean: what if we use latent covariates for detectability?
messages.body_plain:
I had an idea this morning for dealing with variability in detectability (or detectability components) for ecological models in general. I am wondering if anyone else has tried this or has any thoughts on its value. Also, please let me know if there are any existing posts on this approach.

In situations where we are primarily interested in ecological parameters (e.g., abundance, occupancy) and their covariate relationships, and we want to account for spatiotemporal variability in detectability, the two typical approaches are to specify some sort of random effect, include covariates on detectability, or both. Random effects are nice because they can reflect the sampling design and account for lots of different sources of variation, including those that the researcher has not thought of explicitly, but they are computationally expensive. Covariates are nice because they are computationally less expensive and can account for particular sources of variation thought to affect detectability, but the researcher may not have measured all important sources of variation in the form of a covariate.

I am wondering if it could be beneficial and relatively efficient to specify a latent covariate on detectability. I imagine that a latent covariate could account for major axes / sources of variation, including both spatial and temporal sources that have not been explicitly measured in the field, while being less costly in terms of computation and degrees of freedom than random effects.

Does anyone have any thoughts on the potential merits of specifying a latent covariate on detectability (or components of detectability) in terms of both efficacy and computational efficiency? Alternatively or additionally, can you suggest some sources that could provide insight on the merits of trying this out?

messages.body_plain:
Hi Quresh,

I think this ultimately depends on what you mean by a latent covariate. Are you referring to a latent 'grouping' variable (i.e., a finite mixture), where the user allows the model to assign individuals to some finite number of unobservable groups, where those groups would align with the most consistent among-individual similarities of heterogeneity in the data (which could be process or observation variation)? If so, these finite-mixtures have been used to a certain extent in the observational process in the past, but it's definitely not the most widespread type of model used in the mark-recapture field. That being said, the nimble folks and Oliver Gimenez have a recent paper that explores how these finite observational mixture models compare with a non-parametric approach to dealing with heterogeneity in the observational process (i.e., 'broken-stick' models), which is a more readily available model when using nimble. They provide code for each of the different model types. The finite-mixture models can be readily incorporated into JAGS models, but the broken-stick models may require a switch to nimble.

Turek et al. Bayesian non-parametric detection heterogeneity in ecological models. link: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10651-021-00489-1

Although I really like Turek's paper and the model itself, I am not certain that it is computationally more efficient than a random effects model. I think some of the authors are on this listserv, so they may be able to chime in with more insights.

-Dan

Dear Dan, Quresh,

interesting discussion. I think that such latent variables have a wide scope of application in stats. For instance, they have been used by people modeling pair-wise correlations in species occurrence in communities. The TREE paper by Warton et al. gives a nice explanation in their Box 1: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169534715002402
 <https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169534715002402>
So Many Variables: Joint Modeling in Community Ecology - ScienceDirect <https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169534715002402>
Technological advances have enabled a new class of multivariate models for ecology, with the potential now to specify a statistical model for abundances jointly across many taxa, to simultaneously explore interactions across taxa and the response of abundance to environmental variables.
www.sciencedirect.com <http://www.sciencedirect.com>

It sounds like magic: you estimate not only a coefficient of a covariate, but also the covariate values alongside.

I don't have any intuition about whether this construct could be useful for modeling detection heterogeneity, so my usual answer would then be "Simulation is the answer". Perhaps you can simulate a couple of data sets with different patterns in detection probability (specified for instance by covariates and/or random effects), then ignore that info and see whether and how well you can recover part of it using such latent variables ?

Best regards  -- Marc

Hi Quresh,

First, I should've mentioned the Duarte, Link, and Barker (all et al. 2018) papers earlier, they talk quite a bit about similar issues. These models (random effects on p) are pretty much intrinsically not identifiable. I'll try not to go too far down the rabbit hole of what I think about that, but your definition sounds excellent to me!

Regarding fixing the sign, yea, but it's a little bit more complicated than that. I attached a script with some comments. A key thing to note is that you have to either fix the variance of a latent covariate (and the sign of the effect), or fix the effect of a latent covariate. Otherwise the variance and effect perfectly covary (and can covary a bit with the intercept). In the simulation we just fix N so that the variance in p is identifiable.

So if we assume some observation model (ignoring subscripts):

y ~ binomial(N, p)

here is a random effect model for p:

epsilon ~ normal(0, variance)

logit(p) = intercept + epsilon

Here is a latent covariate model with a fixed effect for p:

eta ~ normal(0, variance)

logit(p) = intercept + theta * eta

theta = 1

Those are the same models? I think if you fix the variance you're just re-scaling the covariate (i.e., also the same thing). I attached a very rough draft of a manuscript where we use a latent variable for multiple observed processes (hatch date and prey captures), and then use it as a covariate for different demographic parameters, and there are some other examples in the script that really delve into why some of those problems occur.

Finally (if you're still reading!), Dan (who responded earlier) and I recently published a paper with Marc and Michael where we do something kind of similar to what you're suggesting. We include a random effect for every survey, but we include multiple species in the analysis, and the random effect is shared across species. So the assumption is that whatever weird combination of date, time, observer, local weather is affecting one species affects all of them in the same way around their various species-specific detection intercepts. This could be structured in a SEM kind of approach as well, and I think it's identifiable, but of course if our assumptions about the structure of heterogeneity are incorrect then it will return poor parameter estimates. >
>
>
> First, I should've mentioned the Duarte, Link, and Barker (all et al. 2018) papers earlier, they talk quite a bit about similar issues. These models (random effects on p) are pretty much intrinsically not identifiable. I'll try not to go too far down the rabbit hole of what I think about that, but your definition sounds excellent to me!
>
>
>
> Regarding fixing the sign, yea, but it's a little bit more complicated than that. I attached a script with some comments. A key thing to note is that you have to either fix the variance of a latent covariate (and the sign of the effect), or fix the effect of a latent covariate. Otherwise the variance and effect perfectly covary (and can covary a bit with the intercept). In the simulation we just fix N so that the variance in p is identifiable.
>
>
>
> So if we assume some observation model (ignoring subscripts):
>
> y ~ binomial(N, p)
>
>
>
> here is a random effect model for p:
>
> epsilon ~ normal(0, variance)
>
> logit(p) = intercept + epsilon
>
>
>
> Here is a latent covariate model with a fixed effect for p:
>
> eta ~ normal(0, variance)
>
> logit(p) = intercept + theta * eta
>
> theta = 1
>
>
>
> Those are the same models? I think if you fix the variance you're just re-scaling the covariate (i.e., also the same thing). I attached a very rough draft of a manuscript where we use a latent variable for multiple observed processes (hatch date and prey captures), and then use it as a covariate for different demographic parameters, and there are some other examples in the script that really delve into why some of those problems occur.
>
>
>
> Finally (if you're still reading!), Dan (who responded earlier) and I recently published a paper with Marc and Michael where we do something kind of similar to what you're suggesting. We include a random effect for every survey, but we include multiple species in the analysis, and the random effect is shared across species. So the assumption is that whatever weird combination of date, time, observer, local weather is affecting one species affects all of them in the same way around their various species-specific detection intercepts. This could be structured in a SEM kind of approach as well, and I think it's identifiable, but of course if our assumptions about the structure of heterogeneity are incorrect then it will return poor parameter estimates. Link here:

> > > > > >
> > > > > > In situations where we are primarily interested in ecological parameters (e.g., abundance, occupancy) and their covariate relationships, and we want to account for spatiotemporal variability in detectability, the two typical approaches are to specify some sort of random effect, include covariates on detectability, or both. messages.subject: Re: what if we use latent covariates for detectability?
messages.subject_clean: what if we use latent covariates for detectability?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Quresh,

This is something I've also been interested in and messing around with for a few different multi-species applications where spatial/spatiotemporal variation in the sampling effort within a given site is known or suspected, with good reason to believe all species will not respond the same and some interest in inter-specific detection correlation (sensu some of the papers previously mentioned).  Not sure if this mirrors your motivation and I've not explored modeling decisions (a la Tobler et al. 2019 in Ecology) in any depth, but certainly seem to be benefits associated with dimension reduction relative to random effects for each individual species (structured by site or site*survey).

If this is the sort of thing you were thinking of, just wanted to note that there seem to be mixed schools of thought regarding whether loadings/coefficients should be constrained within the sampling process (certain loadings forced to be positive, whatever) vs. aligned/transformed after the fact. My limited understanding is that the latter tactic is more efficient (blaavan employs it, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.07733.pdf).

Cheers,

John

On Friday, January 21, 2022 at 9:07:03 AM UTC-7 quresh...@birdconservancy.org wrote:
> I had an idea this morning for dealing with variability in detectability (or detectability components) for ecological models in general. I am wondering if anyone else has tried this or has any thoughts on its value. Also, please let me know if there are any existing posts on this approach.
>
> In situations where we are primarily interested in ecological parameters (e.g., abundance, occupancy) and their covariate relationships, and we want to account for spatiotemporal variability in detectability, the two typical approaches are to specify some sort of random effect, include covariates on detectability, or both. Random effects are nice because they can reflect the sampling design and account for lots of different sources of variation, including those that the researcher has not thought of explicitly, but they are computationally expensive. Covariates are nice because they are computationally less expensive and can account for particular sources of variation thought to affect detectability, but the researcher may not have measured all important sources of variation in the form of a covariate.
>
> I am wondering if it could be beneficial and relatively efficient to specify a latent covariate on detectability. I imagine that a latent covariate could account for major axes / sources of variation, including both spatial and temporal sources that have not been explicitly measured in the field, while being less costly in terms of computation and degrees of freedom than random effects.
>
> Does anyone have any thoughts on the potential merits of specifying a latent covariate on detectability (or components of detectability) in terms of both efficacy and computational efficiency? Alternatively or additionally, can you suggest some sources that could provide insight on the merits of trying this out?

Hello all,
Thank you for your time :)
I am fitting a JollySaber model via multi-state and Data augmentation.
The model has 4 hidden states. "not yet enter", "young", "Adult", "Dead".
and 3 observed states: "not seen", "Seen as young", "seen as an adult".

I am trying to model the survival probability as a function of age and other covariates. vial the logit function, for example:
logit(surv)=A_0 + A_1*weight + A_2*Age

The model gives correct estimates for population sizes, but the coefficient of the transition probability between the states Adult and Dead are not consistent. I tried different approaches to treat the non-observed covariates as using a 0, NA (similar modeling as Royle 2009) and using sampled values from my seen covariates. All of them without much luck. Also, I tried different scenarios in my simulated population. All of them without much luck.
Is there something that I may be missing in the modeling of the transition probability?
does anyone have any idea on how to improve the coefficients of the regression model when using DA?

Thank you for your time and comments!

Royle, J. A. (2009). Analysis of capture–recapture models with individual covariates using data augmentation. Biometrics, 65(1), 267-274.
